title: Everyday minor problems
subtitle: a leaking pipe, a chipped cup, a grazed knee
summary: Describe the small things that go wrong every day - broken machines, chipped cups, grazed knees and blocked sinks - with the exact verb English uses for each.

lesson.heading: Things that go wrong in houses and flats
lesson.text: Each kind of damage has its own verb. Something **leaks**, **smashes**, **cracks**, **chips**, **comes off** or **breaks down** - the words are not interchangeable.

examples.text: He kicked the football too hard and it **smashed** a window.
I'm sorry, your cup's **chipped**. Let me get you another one.
The washing machine **broke down** the other day.

lesson.heading: Power and electronics
lesson.text: Batteries **run out** or **go flat**; a whole street can have a **power cut**; and a computer **crashes**.

examples.text: The batteries in this torch have **run out** / are **dead**. I'll have to get some more.
The lights aren't working - there's been a **power cut**.
The car won't start. Perhaps the battery's **flat**.

lesson.heading: Everyday minor injuries
rows: injure it by turning it suddenly: She twisted her ankle coming down the stairs.
hit it against something: I banged my head against the cupboard door.
get a dark area on the skin where you have hurt yourself
almost fall down because you hit your foot against something
make the skin red and broken, but with no blood

lesson.heading: Other everyday problems
lesson.text: A few more useful verbs: to **mislay** something is to put it somewhere and then not be able to find it; a **stain** is a permanent mark; and a **dent** is metal bent a little by a knock.

examples.text: I've **mislaid** my memory stick. Have you seen it anywhere?
She **spilt** some coffee on the carpet. I hope it doesn't leave a **stain**.

examples.note: the water will not run away

examples.text: I'm afraid I've **dented** your car. I'll pay for the repairs.
I've **locked myself out**. Can I use your phone to ring my wife?
The kitchen clock's **slow**. What time d'you make it?

lesson.heading: Same word, two word classes
rows: There's a crack in this pot.
There's a chip in the rim.
I've got a bruise on my leg.
There's a dent in the door.
lesson.note: Flood, bump, bang, graze and lock work the same way. Always note when a word belongs to more than one word class.

lesson.text: Machines **break down**; cups and plates **chip** or **crack**; windows **smash**; batteries **run out** or go **flat**.

exercises.prompt: We had to use candles because there was a ___.
exercises.explanation: A power cut is a period when the electricity supply stops.

exercises.prompt: I didn't look where I was going as I walked through the low doorway and ___ my head.
exercises.explanation: You bump or bang your head against something, and may get a bruise.

exercises.prompt: The wind blew the door shut and I realised I'd locked myself ___.
exercises.explanation: To lock yourself out = to shut the door with the key still inside.

exercises.prompt: I accidentally sat on my bag of crisps and they all got ___.
exercises.explanation: Crushed = pressed so hard that they broke into small pieces.

exercises.prompt: I would ring her but I'm afraid I've ___ her number. She wrote it down for me.
exercises.explanation: To mislay something is to put it somewhere and then be unable to find it.

exercises.prompt: Match each remark with the problem that caused it.

pairs.left: We had to send for a plumber.
I had to call out a local mechanic.
Our neighbours let us use their washing machine.
What type of batteries does it take? I'll get some.
I left it in the oven too long. It's all black now!
I lost all my work - I should have saved it more often!

exercises.prompt: Which is the odd one out: *spill, flood, chip*?
options: chip - the other two involve liquids
spill - the other two are accidents
flood - the other two are small problems
exercises.explanation: Spilling and flooding both involve liquid; chipping is damage to a solid object.

exercises.prompt: Which is the odd one out: *stain, graze, bruise*?
options: stain - the other two are minor injuries
graze - the other two leave marks
bruise - the other two are on the skin
exercises.explanation: A graze and a bruise are minor injuries; a stain is a permanent mark on a surface.

exercises.prompt: Which is the odd one out: *run out, bump, flat*?
options: bump - the other two can be used about batteries
flat - the other two are verbs
run out - the other two are short words
exercises.explanation: Batteries run out or go flat; bump describes hitting part of your body against something.

exercises.prompt: Which is the odd one out: *leak, smash, chip*?
options: leak - the other two are types of damage to solid objects
smash - the other two are quiet
chip - the other two are serious
exercises.explanation: Smashing and chipping damage solid objects; leaking is about liquid escaping.

exercises.prompt: Which noun goes with each problem?

exercises.statement: If you *trip*, you almost fall down because you hit your foot against something.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Kelly tripped and fell down and grazed her knee.

exercises.statement: If a cup is *chipped*, a small piece has broken off the edge.
exercises.explanation: A chipped cup has a small piece missing; a cracked one has a line of damage in it.

exercises.answer: She spilt some coffee on the carpet and it left a stain.
exercises.explanation: A stain is a permanent mark.
